newsitem.title: CANADA: Outgoing president foresees robust growth at WCE.
newsitem.headline: Outgoing president foresees robust growth at WCE.

text.p: Robust growth in trading volume should continue at the Winnipeg Commodity Exchange as deregulation of Canadian agriculture draws more interest in risk management, the WCE's outgoing president told Reuters.

"The changes in the grain and transportation industry have been unequalled in the 102 years before I joined the Exchange with the exception of the introduction of the Board," WCE president Fred Siemens said.
Siemens has presided over the 109-year-old WCE since March 1992. He said Wednesday he will resign at the end of October.
His tenure ends as the Canadian Prairie grain marketing system faces what could be the most sweeping overhaul in its history.

In mid-1992, shortly after Siemens became president of the exchange, barley was removed from the Canadian Wheat Board's export monopoly by cabinet order and traded on the WCE for 40 days. A Supreme Court ruling reinstated the CWB's monopoly in September 1992.
Feed barley is sold on an open market in Canada but exported to the world exclusively by the Canadian Wheat Board. A federal panel in July recommended an open market in exports.
Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale will announce his decision on that recommendation later Friday.
"Feed wheat and barley combined can match the volume traded in canola (on the exchange)," Siemens predicted.
Canola, an oilseed used in cooking oil and margarine, is the most actively traded commodity in Winnipeg with 108,490 contracts changing hands last month.
Volume of trade in feed barley reached 25,456 contracts and feed wheat was 29,500 contracts, for a total of 54,956 contracts.
Canada's barley crop is three times larger than canola.
The WCE redesigned all of its contracts last year, in large part due to the elimination of Canada's multi-million dollar rail freight subsidy.

Memphis-based analytical firm Sparks Companies Inc found domestic and international users of the WCE's redesigned feed barley contract monitored the instrument closely and said it tracked international cash prices.
"Sparks said there's no reason barley volume can't exceed canola's volume, even with the status quo," Siemens said.
The WCE is already working with the CWB in drafting the world's first durum wheat futures contract.
It is also studying the feasibility of a hog contract following deregulation of the hog industry in Manitoba July 1.

Siemens said the coming months and years will be challenging ones for his successor with the repercussions of changes in the industry, and it was time for him to step aside to allow someone with new ideas set the direction of the WCE.
He leaves the exchange to work with an electronic cash commodity brokerage firm in Calgary, Alberta.
